extracted.intended_audience: educated general reading public (early-18th-century Spectator readership); writers of periodical moral/social essays
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, moralizing/satirical periodical essays (Spectator-style) that comment on social behaviour, domestic relations, patronage, and courtly life using letters, anecdotes, and observant description. Emphasis on exposing vices and advising readers through examples and character sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate dedication / patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedications to ignorant Men are as absurd as any of the Speeches of Bulfinch in the Droll: Such an Address ... one is apt to translate into other Words; and when the Different Parties are thoroughly considered, the Panegyrick generally implies no more than if the Author should say to the Patron; My very good Lord, You and I can never understand one another, therefore I humbly desire we may be intimate Friends for the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not direct or dedicate learned or ingenious work to patrons who do not appreciate liberal arts; a dedication to an ignorant patron appears ridiculous and insincere. Choose patrons who understand and merit the praise you bestow, because the audience will read the dedication as revealing the relationship rather than genuine esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise engages the praiser's reputation (be cautious whom you commend)
rubrics_metrics.description: He that commends another engages so much of his own Reputation as he gives to that Person commended; and he that has nothing laudable in himself is not of Ability to be such a Surety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should weigh the consequences of praising others: commendation acts as a vouch; praising an unworthy person damages the author's own standing. Avoid enthusiastic endorsements of people who lack virtue or merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satirical exposure to deter vice
rubrics_metrics.description: I have exposed this Picture of an unnatural Father with the same Intention, that its Deformity may deter others from its Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moral instruction is the aim, vividly portraying the deformity of vice (through caricature, example, or comic portrait) can serve to deter imitation. Satirical exposure should make the vice repulsive so readers are discouraged from similar conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer virtue over outward wealth when choosing exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vulgar and Men of Sense agree in admiring Men for having what they themselves would rather be possessed of; the wise Man applauds him whom he thinks most virtuous; the rest of the World, him who is most wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In essays and moral commentary, emphasise virtue and moral worth rather than mere possession or rank. Critique the common tendency to admire wealth and external advantages instead of true merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters, billets, and direct speech as a rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall conclude this Paper with a Billet which has fallen into my Hands ... The Author of it had formerly been her Lover. When all Possibility of Commerce between them on the Subject of Love was cut off, she spoke so handsomely of him, as to give Occasion for this Letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating fictional or real-seeming letters and direct speech can serve as an effective rhetorical device to reveal character, expose hypocrisy, and provide concrete examples. Letters allow irony and dramatic contrast (e.g., a father's brutal letter) to speak for themselves without overt authorial moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict social rituals through concrete, often comic, detail to satirize vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The famous Doctor in Moorfields ... This Method was kept in respect to all other Passions and Concerns, and the skilful Waiter below sifted the Enquirer ... The Levée of a great Man is laid after the same manner ... There are several Ways of making this first Appearance: you may be either half dressed, and washing your self, which is indeed the most stately ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To satirize courtly vanity or social affectation, focus on small, concrete gestures and scenography (dress, posture, whispers, servants' signals). These particulars render the absurdities of social ritual visible and amusing, and allow implicit critique through described behavior rather than abstract denunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show parental virtue/defect through the conduct of offspring (character contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Habits are what will certainly improve a Man's Fortune and Reputation; but on the other side, Affluence of Fortune will not as probably produce good Affections of the Mind ... I know not how to express it, but I think I may call it a transplanted Self-love. ... I shall end this Rhapsody with a Letter to an excellent young Man of my Acquaintance, who has lately lost a worthy Father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exploring legacy and moral education in essays or short fiction, use contrasting portraits of children (virtuous daughter vs. profligate son) to illustrate the quality of a parent's life and influence. Concrete scenes of conduct are more persuasive than abstract claims about inheritance or reputation.
